title: Exponential Quantum Speedup in Simulating Coupled Classical Oscillators
authors: Ryan Babbush (Google Quantum AI, USA), Dominic W. Berry (Macquarie University, Australia), Robin Kothari (Google Quantum AI, USA), Rolando D. Somma (Google Quantum AI, USA), Nathan Wiebe (University of Toronto; Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, Canada; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, USA)
abstract: We study the problem of simulating the time evolution of a system of $2^n$ classical coupled oscillators (e.g., $2^n$ balls connected by springs) on a quantum computer. We map Newton's equation for harmonic potentials to Schr\”odinger's equation, such that the amplitudes of an $\cO(n)$-qubit quantum state encode the momenta and displacements of the $2^n$ classical oscillators. Given oracle access to the masses and spring constants, we describe a quantum algorithm with query and time complexity $\poly(n)$ that solves this problem when certain parameters are polynomially bounded and the initial state is easy to prepare. As an example application, we apply our quantum algorithm to efficiently estimate the normalized kinetic energy of an oscillator at any time. We then show that any classical algorithm solving the same problem must make $2^{\Omega(n)}$ queries to the oracle and we also show that when the oracles are instantiated by $\poly(n)$-size circuits, the problem is \BQP-complete. Thus, our approach solves a potentially practical application with an exponential speedup over classical computers.

In this paper we provide a new example of a problem that
yields a provable exponential quantum advantage: the simulation of a computational problem from Newtonian mechanics, or
classical mechanics. To make this paper accessible to a broad
range of readers, we review all the Newtonian mechanics
required to understand this paper in Sec. I-A. For now, we
simply explain the problem at an intuitive level. In the simplest
version of the problem, we have N balls, with any pair of balls
potentially connected by a spring. Figure 1 shows an example
of such a system with N = 8 with adjacent balls connected
by springs and the balls on the boundary connected to a wall.

Abstract—We study the problem of simulating the time
evolution of a system of 2n classical coupled oscillators (e.g.,
2n balls connected by springs) on a quantum computer. We
map Newton’s equation for harmonic potentials to Schrödinger’s
equation, such that the amplitudes of an O(n)-qubit quantum
state encode the momenta and displacements of the 2n classical
oscillators. Given oracle access to the masses and spring constants,
we describe a quantum algorithm with query and time complexity
poly(n) that solves this problem when certain parameters are
polynomially bounded and the initial state is easy to prepare.
As an example application, we apply our quantum algorithm to
efﬁciently estimate the normalized kinetic energy of an oscillator
at any time. We then show that any classical algorithm solving
the same problem must make 2Ω(n) queries to the oracle and we
also show that when the oracles are instantiated by poly(n)-size
circuits, the problem is BQP-complete. Thus, our approach solves
a potentially practical application with an exponential speedup
over classical computers.
Index Terms—quantum algorithm, exponential speedup, BQPcomplete, harmonic oscillators

I. I NTRODUCTION

Fig. 1. An example of N = 8 balls connected by springs in one dimension.

Simulating the time evolution of a quantum system, also
known as the Hamiltonian simulation problem, is one of the
most promising uses of a quantum computer [2]. This is
because it has many practical applications and it is unlikely
that there is an efﬁcient classical algorithm for Hamiltonian
simulation since it is BQP-complete.1 If there were an efﬁcient
classical algorithm for Hamiltonian simulation, it would also
imply efﬁcient classical algorithms for all problems in BQP,
including (for example) integer factorization [3]. Hamiltonian
simulation algorithms lead to exponential advantage for a
number of applications spanning simulation of chemistry [4],
simulation of quantum ﬁeld theory [5], solving linear systems
and differential equations [6], [7] and applications to quantum
walk algorithms [8]. However, the number of cases where we

Given the mass of each ball and the strength of each spring
(known as its spring constant), Newton’s equation of motion
yields a set of differential equations that must be satisﬁed by
the (time-dependent) positions and velocities of the balls. Using
these equations, and given the initial positions and velocities
of each ball, their ﬁnal positions and velocities are uniquely
determined (i.e., the solution to this system of differential
equations exists and is unique). The computational complexity
of solving this problem is the focus of this work.
This setup straightforwardly deﬁnes a computational problem,
where the inputs are the N masses, O(N 2 ) spring constants,
N initial positions and velocities, and a time t, and the outputs
are the N ﬁnal positions and velocities. Since the outputs are
of size N , this problem requires Ω(N ) time to solve on a
classical or quantum computer.
Instead of this formulation, we want to deﬁne a version of
this problem where we view N = 2n as being exponentially
large, and our inputs and outputs are speciﬁed succinctly and

are of size poly(n).2 Since the problem needs to have outputs
of size poly(n), we cannot simply output the positions and
velocities of all balls. Nevertheless, we formulate problems
where the output contains interesting global properties of the
system, such as kinetic and potential energies of parts of the
system. After imposing some additional requirements on certain
input parameters being polynomially bounded, we ﬁnally arrive
at a formally deﬁned problem with inputs and outputs of size
poly(n). With such a speciﬁcation, there is hope of solving
the problem in time poly(n). We then prove that this problem
can be solved in poly(n) time on a quantum computer, and
hence the problem is in BQP. The problems we study and our
main results are described in Sec. I-B.
Since we have added constraints on the inputs, and the
outputs contain less information than all the positions and
velocities, it is natural to wonder if the resulting problem we
have deﬁned is now easy to solve classically. We show that
this is not the case by showing that the problem described
above is BQP-complete. Our algorithms also work when the
inputs are speciﬁed by an oracle, instead of being described
succinctly. For this version of the problem, we show that any
classical algorithm must make exponentially many queries to
the oracle.
Although we use it as the main motivating system, note
that our algorithms do not apply merely to balls connected
by springs. This is a special case of a ubiquitous system
in physics known as the harmonic oscillator, and essentially
the same equations describe a variety of physical phenomena
including: networks of masses and springs [10], circuits with
capacitors and inductors [11], models of neuron activity [12],
and vibrations in molecules [13], materials, and mechanical
structures. More generally, any classical system described by a
conservative force (i.e., a force where it is possible to deﬁne a
notion of potential energy) can be approximated using the
same set of equations for small perturbations near stable
equilibrium. Since gravitational and electrostatic forces are
examples of conservative forces, many physical systems can
be approximated in this way.
Our algorithm, formally described in Sec. II-A, is based
on mapping the system of differential equations we want to
solve to the Hamiltonian simulation problem, combined with
other quantum algorithmic primitives like phase estimation
and block encodings. The Hamiltonian simulation problem
also involves simulating the time evolution of a system, but
the system is quantum. Here, the time evolution is described
by the Schrödinger equation, which is a homogeneous, ﬁrstorder partial differential equation. The harmonic oscillator is
deﬁned by a second-order ordinary differential equation. At
ﬁrst glance it is not obvious that one can be mapped to the
other. However, as we show, this can be done by deﬁning an
appropriate quantum Hamiltonian from the classical system.
There is already prior work in solving other differential
equations on a quantum computer, such as [7], [14], [15],

which employ quantum linear systems algorithms [6], [16],
[17]. More closely related to our work are approaches based
on Hamiltonian simulation, such as [18]–[20], which have so
far only succeeded in obtaining polynomial speedups.
Our oracular lower bound described in Sec. III is proved by
showing that the glued trees problem of Childs et al. [8] is
a special case of our problem. Speciﬁcally, we put a ball of
unit mass at every node in the glued trees graph and a spring
of unit spring constant at every edge of the glued trees graph.
With this setup, we start with all the balls at rest, except the
entrance vertex of the glued trees graph has unit velocity. We
show that after a polynomial amount of time, the exit vertex of
the graph will have at least inverse polynomial velocity, which
our algorithm can detect.
Our BQP-hardness result described in Sec. IV uses a
modiﬁed version of the Feynman–Kitaev circuit-to-Hamiltonian
construction [21], [22]. A straightforward application of the
construction yields a quantum Hamiltonian that may not, in
general, arise from a classical system of balls and springs. For
example, one issue is that spring constants and masses are
non-negative numbers, but this construction in general leads
to complex and negative numbers in the resulting Hamiltonian.
However, we are able to modify the construction to show that
the success probability of an arbitrary poly(n) size quantum
circuit can be mapped to the normalized kinetic energy of
one of the balls, which can be estimated by our algorithm
efﬁciently.
A. Newtonian mechanics
We now describe the classical system we study in detail
without assuming much familiarity with the subject. Readers
who are familiar with harmonic oscillators may skim this
section to understand our notation.
a) A single oscillator.: As a warm up, imagine we have
only one ball of mass m > 0. While we have called this a
“ball” so far, formally it is a point mass, i.e., a point in space
that has some mass, and we will call it a mass or oscillator
from now on. Let the oscillator be connected to a wall by
a spring of spring constant κ ≥ 0, which is a measure of
the strength of the spring. Assume the oscillator lives in a
one-dimensional space as in Fig. 1. Then let x ∈ R denote
the oscillator’s displacement from its rest position. I.e., when
x = 0, the oscillator is at rest and the spring applies no force on
it. Hooke’s law, which describes the force applied by a spring
when compressed or extended, states that when the oscillator
is displaced by x, the force acting on it will be −κx. The
negative sign tells us that the force is in the opposite direction
of the displacement, i.e., it is a restorative force trying to bring
the oscillator back to its rest position.
If we let x(t) denote the oscillator’s position at time t,
then the acceleration of the oscillator at time t is its second
derivative, ẍ(t).3 Combining Newton’s second law of motion

Our goal is to formulate a problem of simulating the time
dynamics of N = 2n oscillators efﬁciently, i.e., in time
polylog(N ) = poly(n). Doing so requires a particular notion
of “simulation”, since any algorithm that outputs the full vectors
x(t) or x˙ (t) would necessarily have complexity at least linear
in N . For maximum generality we will assume oracles for
certain inputs, although they can also be instantiated by circuits
of size poly(n), as we later do.
For the input M, we simply assume an oracle that on input
j outputs mj . For the matrix K, we will assume it is d-sparse
(i.e., there are at most d non-zero entries in each row) and
use a standard oracle for d-sparse matrices used in quantum
algorithms. These oracles are described in detail in the full
version of this paper [1], including a discussion of the bits of
precision output by each oracle.
Since we want to input and output exponentially many
positions and velocities, we will store them in the amplitudes
of a quantum state. A naive encoding where each amplitude
encodes either a position or velocity will lead to a quantum state
whose norm is a function of time, since there is no particular
reason that the sum of squares of positions and velocities is
constant. However, as we just discussed, the total energy of
the system is conserved. Hence we can deﬁne a quantum state
whose amplitudes are the square roots of the terms that appear
in K(t) + U (t), which will mean its norm will not depend on
time. Speciﬁcally, we consider a quantum state with amplitudes

The query lower bound stated in Thm. 2 follows from a

IV. BQP- COMPLETENESS
A relevant question is whether our quantum algorithm results
in a quantum speedup or if it can be efﬁciently simulated by
classical algorithms. We address this question by showing that
our approach can simulate any quantum circuit of size L acting
on q qubits in time that is polynomial in L and q. More precisely
we show that Problem 3 is BQP-complete, thereby proving
Thm. 3. This is strong evidence that no polynomial-time (in n)
classical algorithm for simulating systems of coupled classical
oscillators exists. Our result also adds a new problem to the
list of “natural” BQP-complete problems [33].
To prove this, we start from the standard BQP-complete
problem of simulating universal quantum circuits, i.e., the
problem of determining some property of the output state
⊗q
|φ = UL . . . U1 |0 , where L = poly(q). The unitary gates
Ul belong to a universal set such as {H, X, Toﬀ}, where
H and X are single-qubit Hadamard and Pauli X (bit ﬂip)
gates, and Toff is the three-qubit Toffoli gate. (Without loss
of generality, all Hadamard gates can act on the last qubit, a
property that is not necessary but we use it to simplify the
presentation of the proof.) The speciﬁc problem is that of
deciding if |φ is essentially the all zero state or has almost
no overlap on it. In the full version of this paper [1], we show
that this problem reduces to one in which the kinetic energy
of a speciﬁc oscillator is either exponentially close to zero
or at least 1/poly(q) large. This is essentially Problem 3 for
n = O(q).
